questions.stem: Within two milliseconds, the -XX:+PrintCompilation log of an order service prints `412   88       3       Order::total (54 bytes)`, then `413   91       4       Order::total (54 bytes)`, then `414   88       3       Order::total (54 bytes)   made not entrant`. No later line mentions Order::total. Where does a call to Order::total made at this point run?

options.text: In compile 91, since compile 88 stopped taking calls once a newer compile of the method could take them
options.says: a lower tier made not entrant after a higher tier of the same method was installed is a replacement; new calls enter the newest code

options.text: In the interpreter, since compile 88 was thrown away and the method has to be profiled again before C2 compiles it
options.says: made not entrant on a lower tier is usually a replacement; compile 91 is live and takes the calls

options.text: In compile 88, since a tier-4 compile only takes over a method's loops and its calls stay in tier-3 code
options.says: a loop (OSR) compile is marked with % and an @ bytecode index; compile 91 is an ordinary compile that takes calls

options.text: In the interpreter, since made not entrant means an assumption broke and the method's compiled code was all discarded
options.says: the same words appear when a newer compile replaces older code; only a compile with nothing newer to take its place sends calls back

origin.section: A Method Starts in the Interpreter and Is Compiled in Tiers Once Its Counters Say It Is Hot

questions.stem: A benchmark's main() calls parseAll() five times and times each call. parseAll() contains one loop of 50 million iterations. In a fresh JVM the times are 9 ms, 11 ms, 4 ms, 4 ms and 4 ms. What best explains the 11 ms of the second call?

options.text: The loop's C2 code was compiled only for staying in the loop, so leaving it in the first call sent the method back to slower code
options.says: the OSR compile had never seen the loop exit, so leaving the loop hit a trap and the next call started in tier-3 code until C2 compiled the method itself

options.text: The loop's C2 code was installed during the first call, so the second call paid for C2 profiling the loop from the start
options.says: profiling happens in the interpreter and in tier-3 C1 code; C2 compiles from that profile and does not profile itself

options.text: The loop ran entirely in the interpreter in the second call, since a method is compiled only once it has returned enough times
options.says: loop iterations count too, and an OSR compile switches a running call into compiled code mid-loop

options.text: The loop ran entirely in tier-1 code in the second call, since tier-1 code is what a method gets once its first call has finished
options.says: tier 1 is plain C1 code for trivial methods such as getters; a hot loop goes through tier 3 to tier 4

origin.section: Until the Compiled Code Is Installed, the Same Loop Runs Tens of Times Slower

questions.stem: In a pricing engine, the hot method price(Rule r) calls r.apply(order). Rule is a class, and no loaded class overrides apply. At noon, a tenant's plug-in class that extends Rule and overrides apply is loaded with Class.forName; no request calls it yet. What happens to price's tier-4 code?

options.text: It is made not entrant as the class loads, since it relied on apply having a single implementation
options.says: C2 called the only implementation directly and recorded a dependency on it; loading an overriding class invalidates the code, and C2 compiles price again once it is hot

options.text: It is made not entrant at the first call that passes the plug-in, since it checks the receiver's class at each call
options.says: that is how the call behaved with an interface; with a class and one implementation, C2 relied on the class hierarchy, and the load alone invalidated it

options.text: It keeps running, since a class that no request has called leaves compiled code as it was
options.says: the compiled code depended on apply having one implementation; the load broke that assumption

options.text: It keeps running, since C2 code for a method stays installed until the process restarts
options.says: compiled code is made not entrant when an assumption breaks; on the page the load invalidated total's tier-4 code at once

origin.section: Compiled Code Rests on Assumptions, and a Class Loaded Later Can Make It Not Entrant

questions.stem: A benchmark times `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += discount(1999);` with discount a short arithmetic method, prints sum at the end, and reports 0.01 ns per call after warm-up. Under -Xint the same loop takes 15 ns per call. What does the 0.01 ns measure?

options.text: Almost nothing, since the argument 1999 is the same on every iteration and the JIT computed the call's value once
options.says: with a constant input the JIT can compute the call once; the loop is left adding a constant

options.text: Almost nothing, since the additions all go into one local, sum, and the JIT removed the loop as unused work
options.says: adding results into a sum that is printed uses them; the work disappeared because the input never changed

options.text: The cost of discount once compiled, since every result is added into sum, which is printed, so none can be removed
options.says: using every result is necessary but not enough: a constant input lets the JIT compute the value once

options.text: The cost of discount once compiled, since the 15 ns under -Xint is mostly overhead that compiled code never pays
options.says: the interpreter's overhead explains part of the gap, but 0.01 ns is under one CPU cycle, so the work itself is gone

origin.section: A Benchmark Measures Nothing When the JIT Can Drop the Work or Fold Its Input
